We congratulate ourselves on closing down peat stations and reducing our herd numbers while importing product from jurisdictions with far weaker environmental standards, produced with a far higher carbon footprint, and shipped halfway around the world. That is not climate action; it is climate accountancy of the most dishonest kind. Meanwhile, ordinary families in this country are being asked to carry the cost. The carbon tax increases fall hardest on people in rural Ireland who have no alternative to the private car, who depend on solid fuel or oil to heat their homes because the Government has failed to deliver the retrofitting programme at anything like the pace required. A person on a low income in Leitrim or Roscommon does not have the option of hopping on the Luas. There is no bus. There is no rail service worth talking about. So they pay, and they pay again, while multinational corporations and international shipping and aviation continue largely untouched. If the Government were serious, it would invest in public transport in rural areas before penalising people for not using services that do not exist. It would front-load the retrofitting of local authority housing. It would take on the vested interests at European and global level instead of lecturing pensioners about their fuel. I ask the Minister directly: what proportion of the carbon tax revenue collected to date has actually been returned to the communities most affected? What analysis has the Department done of the distributional impact of these measures on rural households? Until those questions are answered honestly, the Government's climate policy will rightly be seen for what it is - tokenism dressed up as ambition, penalising our own people while the real polluters carry on regardless.

That is not rhetoric; that is concrete investment in the communities the member claims to speak for. When we came into office, the auto sector in this country had been hollowed out by years of neglect under the previous government. Plants were closing. Investment was flowing south. What we have done, working with provinces of all political stripes and with organized labour, is position Canada as a destination of choice for the industries of the future. We have secured historic investments in battery manufacturing, in critical minerals processing, in clean steel and aluminum. These are not abstractions. These are jobs in Windsor, in Oshawa, in St. Thomas, in communities across Ontario and indeed across the country. The member opposite would have Canadians believe that everything is broken, that nothing works, that there is no hope. That is the entirety of his party's message. But when we actually look at the record, Canada has recovered jobs faster than almost any of our G7 partners. Unemployment remains near historic lows. Wages are growing. Is there more work to do? Of course there is. Affordability pressures are real, and no one on this side of the House pretends otherwise. That is precisely why we brought forward the measures in this legislation: to help families with the cost of living, to build more homes faster, and to keep investing in the industries that will pay the bills of tomorrow. What I would ask the hon. member is this: if he is so concerned about workers, why did he and his party vote against every single one of these investments? Why did they vote against the dental care that is now helping seniors in his own riding? Canadians deserve better than a party that talks down their country while voting against its future.

I have been very clear that we learned lessons from last year. The calculated grades process, whatever its imperfections, was put together at speed in an emergency, and the State Examinations Commission, the Department and thousands of teachers did extraordinary work to make it happen. Students have had enough uncertainty. When we make the announcement, it will be one we can deliver. I also want to acknowledge directly what students have been through. This cohort lost significant portions of fifth year and sixth year. They have studied at kitchen tables, over broken broadband connections, without the ordinary supports of school life. Whatever mechanism we arrive at must recognise that reality, and there will be fairness built into the examinations themselves - adjustments to the papers, greater choice within them, so that no student is disadvantaged for material that could not be covered. The well-being supports in schools have been enhanced, and guidance counsellors are available to every student. I say to the Deputies opposite that I share their urgency. We will bring clarity at the earliest possible date, but it will be clarity that holds, and the interests of students - their health, their futures and their fair treatment - will be at the centre of every decision we take.

It could include reintegration programmes for former combatants, particularly child soldiers, giving them education, skills and a route back into civilian life. It could include trauma counselling and reconciliation work of the kind we have seen bear fruit in Rwanda and in Colombia. It could include support for independent media and for civil society organisations that hold fragile governments to account and give communities a voice other than the gun. These interventions are extraordinarily cheap relative to the alternative. The Institute for Economics and Peace has estimated that every pound spent on peacebuilding saves many multiples of that in the costs of conflict - in humanitarian response, in peacekeeping deployments, in lost trade and in the long shadow that war casts over development. Prevention is not only morally superior to cure; it is fiscally prudent. That is why I am concerned that the proportion of our aid budget devoted to conflict prevention remains so modest, and why the reductions we have seen risk being a false economy of the worst kind. When we withdraw from these programmes, the space we vacate does not remain empty. Others fill it - actors whose interests are not stability, not democracy and not the welfare of the populations concerned. My hon. Friend mentioned the church organisations, and I want to pay particular tribute to them, because they stay. When the agencies pull out and the embassies draw down, the churches and the faith networks remain embedded in their communities, trusted on all sides, able to carry messages across lines that no diplomat can cross. Any strategy that does not harness that reach is leaving one of our most effective instruments unused, and I hope the Minister will address that point directly when he responds.

Mr Hallett has written several volumes setting out his case, has adopted the style "King John II", and has attracted a small but devoted following online who regard the entire royal succession since 1910 as fraudulent. I mention him not to mock him - although the temptation is considerable - but because his case illustrates precisely the point I am seeking to make about this Bill. The law as it stands provides no sensible mechanism for dealing with claims of this kind. They are absurd, but absurdity has never been a barrier to litigation, and each such claim consumes court time, public money and the patience of officials who must respond to correspondence generated in industrial quantities. The second point his case illustrates is the ease with which conspiracy narratives now find an audience. A generation ago, Mr Hallett's theories would have circulated among a handful of correspondents. Today they reach tens of thousands through social media, are repackaged by others, and merge into the wider ecosystem of misinformation that this House has debated many times. When people can be persuaded that the monarchy itself is a century-long fraud, we should not be surprised that they can be persuaded that elections are stolen or vaccines are poison. The remedy is not censorship - I want to be very clear about that. The remedy is a legal framework that disposes of vexatious claims efficiently, and an education system that equips citizens to weigh evidence. The Bill before us makes progress on the first of these, and I support it for that reason, but I say to the Minister that the second is the harder and the more important task. I hope that when she responds she will say something about what the Government are doing beyond the narrow confines of this Bill, because Mr Hallett, harmless as he may be, is a symptom of something that is not harmless at all.

many bills in this place that were labelled as steps toward reconciliation while the substantive issues - clean drinking water, housing, child welfare, the implementation of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission's calls to action - remain unresolved year after year. Of the 94 calls to action, only a small fraction have been fully implemented, and that is not my assessment; that is the assessment of indigenous organizations that track this work carefully. So when we speak of reconciliation in this chamber, we have to ask ourselves whether we are describing a genuine transformation in the relationship or simply borrowing the vocabulary of transformation while the machinery of the status quo grinds on. A nation-to-nation relationship means that indigenous peoples are not stakeholders to be consulted after the decisions are made; they are governments to be negotiated with before the decisions are made. It means free, prior and informed consent is treated as a standard to be met, not an obstacle to be managed. It means that when a court orders compensation for children harmed by a discriminatory child welfare system, the government's response is to pay, not to litigate. I supported this bill at second reading and I will support it again, because incremental progress is still progress and the communities affected have asked us to pass it. But I do not want my support to be mistaken for satisfaction. The member for Kenora is right to warn us about buzzwords. Words like reconciliation carry weight only when they are attached to resources, to timelines and to accountability. I would ask the government, through you, Madam Speaker, to tell this House when it will bring forward a full implementation plan with dates and dollars attached, because until it does, indigenous communities are entitled to their skepticism, and frankly, so are the rest of us. We owe them more than good intentions; we owe them results that can be measured.

Our schools are asking parents for donations to buy basic supplies. Our NHS entered the winter with record waiting lists. Social care is in a state of permanent crisis that the Government have promised to fix in every Queen's Speech and fixed in none. And where is the plan for growth? Productivity has flatlined. Business investment has stalled. The Government's own forecasts show growth being revised down year after year, and their answer is a Finance Bill that tinkers at the margins while the fundamentals rot. My constituents do not experience the economy the Chancellor describes at the Dispatch Box. They experience the economy of insecure work, of zero-hours contracts, of choosing between heating and eating. Until a Budget speaks to that reality, it does not deserve the name of an economic plan. For those reasons, I shall oppose this Bill tonight, and I urge Members on the Benches opposite who know in their hearts that their constituencies are suffering the same neglect to join us in the Lobby.

The additional reservoir will provide the storage headroom needed so that when a burst occurs - and on a main of that age, bursts will continue to occur - there is sufficient reserve to maintain supply while repairs are carried out. That is why I am pressing Irish Water and the Minister for a definitive timeline: when will planning be lodged, when will the contract be awarded, and when will the reservoir be operational? Communities have heard promises before. The original commitment was given several years ago and the completion date has slipped repeatedly. I am also asking that, in the interim, Irish Water upgrade the vulnerable sections of the existing main, because it makes no sense to wait for the reservoir while the same pipe bursts again and again at the same locations. What they cannot accept is drift, and I will continue to raise this matter until the water flows reliably from every tap.

A justice system earns public confidence when it balances rehabilitation with accountability, and when it never, ever loses sight of the people who have been harmed. That balance has been lost. Victims are not informed of parole hearings in time to participate. They learn of transfers from the news. They are retraumatized at every stage by processes designed around the convenience of institutions rather than the dignity of the people those institutions failed. The bill before us is an opportunity to begin restoring that balance, and that is why I will be supporting measures that strengthen victims' rights to information, to participation and to protection. But legislation is only as good as its implementation, and implementation requires resources and political will. I say to the minister: meet with the families. Sit across the table from the parents of murdered children and explain the current system to their faces. If the government cannot defend its policies in that room, it should not be defending them in this one. Our first obligation is to the innocent, and it is time this Parliament acted like it.

many respects, local authorities have been stripped of their powers over decades - water services gone, waste collection gone, housing delivery reduced to a fraction of what councils once built - and each removal has been justified as efficiency, yet each has left communities with less say over the services they depend on. The members of local authorities, the councillors, are the people closest to the ground. They know every road, every estate, every family in difficulty, and they are the first port of call when something goes wrong. Yet we have starved them of resources and treated them as little more than a consultative afterthought. If this Bill genuinely restores functions and respect to local government, it will have my full support, but I want to raise a number of specific points. First, powers without funding are a trap. If we assign new responsibilities to councils without a commensurate and ring-fenced funding stream, we are setting them up to fail and setting communities up for disappointment. The local property tax, as currently structured, does not give councils a genuine independent revenue base, and the equalisation arrangements penalise some counties in ways that are hard to defend. Second, the workforce issue must be addressed. Councils cannot recruit and retain engineers, planners and housing staff when the private sector and central government agencies outbid them. Third, I ask the Minister to look again at the balance of power between the executive and the elected members. Too many decisions are made by management and merely noted by councillors. Reversing that drift would do more for local democracy than any structural reform. Finally, I want to acknowledge the councillors of all parties and none who do this work for modest recompense and considerable abuse. If we are serious about the ambitions of this Bill, we must make local public life something we encourage good people to enter, not something we make impossible for them.

Turning to the substance of the question, the hon. Member raises the arrangements for Divisions more generally, and I understand the concerns that have been expressed on both sides of the House. Members' time is not unlimited, and lengthy queues take Members away from Committee work, from constituency correspondence and from the Chamber itself. The Procedure Committee has looked at these matters before and I have no doubt it will look at them again. If the hon. Member wishes to make a submission, I would encourage him to do so, and I will draw the attention of the Chair of the Committee to the points raised today. What I would resist is any suggestion that occasional mechanical failure is an argument for wholesale change. Any system - traditional or electronic - will fail from time to time; the test is how quickly it recovers, and by that test the House authorities acquitted themselves well. I would also gently say that the Division system, whatever its inconveniences, brings Members of all parties into physical proximity twice or more a day, and a great deal of the useful business of this House - the quiet word with a Minister, the cross-party conversation that ripens into an amendment - happens in those queues. We should be careful what we optimise away. But the hon. Member has raised a fair point in a fair manner, and it will be considered through the proper channels.

We listened carefully to that feedback, and the Government amendments in this group respond directly to it. The concern, in essence, was that the grounds for removal as originally drafted were too narrow and might not capture every circumstance in which an arbitrator's continued involvement would undermine confidence in the process - for example, where a conflict of interest emerges only after appointment, or where an arbitrator becomes unable to act through illness or other incapacity. The amendments therefore clarify and broaden those grounds while retaining the essential safeguard that removal is not at the whim of either party. That safeguard matters, because the integrity of the arbitration process depends on arbitrators being able to reach decisions without fear that an unwelcome ruling will cost them their position. We are seeking a careful balance: arbitrators must be independent, but they must also be accountable, and the bodies that appoint them must be able to act when something has genuinely gone wrong. I believe these amendments strike that balance. I should also say a word about the wider engagement on this Bill, because the arbitration provisions have benefited enormously from the expertise of practitioners. As well as the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors, we have heard from the Chartered Institute of Arbitrators, from property litigation specialists and from representatives of both landlords and tenants. It is fair to say that neither side of that particular relationship got everything it wanted from this Bill, which the House may take as some evidence that we have landed in a reasonable place. The scheme is designed to be quick, proportionate and final, so that businesses that have survived the pandemic are not now dragged under by protracted disputes over rent arrears that neither party truly has the resources to litigate. I commend the amendments in this group to the House, and I will of course respond to points raised by hon. Members in the debate.

Shannon has the longest runway in the country, a deep-rooted aviation cluster, thousands of acres of zoned and serviced land, and a location that positions it perfectly as a transatlantic gateway. The future mobility campus the Tánaiste visited is proof of what local initiative can achieve. But local initiative can only go so far without national backing. Balanced regional development has been promised in every programme for Government in my lifetime, and the census figures show what has actually happened: relentless concentration on the east coast, with all the overheating that brings - the housing crisis, the congestion, the childcare shortages - while the west and mid-west operate below their potential. That is bad for Dublin and bad for the rest of the country alike. So I am asking the Minister for specific commitments: designated capital funding for the Shannon estuary strategy, delivery of the promised upgrades to the rail connection, and a mandate for the IDA to prioritise the region for the next wave of investment. The potential is not in question. What is in question is whether this Government will match the ambition that the region has already shown for itself.

That is the core purpose: traceability in the service of safety. The information retained would include the technical specifications of the device, its certification history, the identity of the responsible economic operator, and records of any modifications made after installation. Members of the Committee asked, quite reasonably, why this level of detail is necessary and whether it imposes a disproportionate burden, particularly on smaller operators. I want to address that directly. The burden of recording information at the point of manufacture or installation is modest - much of it is data the operator must generate anyway for certification purposes - but the cost of not having it, when something goes wrong, is enormous. We have seen in other sectors what happens when a safety issue emerges and the paper trail is inadequate: months are lost identifying which products are affected, public confidence collapses, and the eventual remediation costs many multiples of what prevention would have cost. The system is designed on a "record once, use many times" principle, so that the same entry serves certification, market surveillance and enforcement functions without duplication. Subsection (6), which we will come to, provides the data protection safeguards: information is retained only as long as necessary, access is restricted to those with a regulatory need, and personal data is minimised - it is devices we are tracking, not individuals. I would also draw the Committee's attention to the consultation responses, which showed strong support from industry for a single national system in preference to the patchwork of voluntary schemes that exists at present. A level playing field, clearly understood obligations and one place to look: that is what the provision delivers, and I commend it to the Committee.

However, on reading the record afterwards, I found the response was somewhat more qualified than it had appeared in the moment, and I want to pin down exactly where the Government stands. Directly elected mayors are not a novelty or an experiment; they are the norm across Europe and in cities we compete with for investment. A mayor with a five-year mandate, real executive powers and a budget can drive housing delivery, transport planning and economic development in a way that a rotating ceremonial office simply cannot. The management system we have, whereby unelected officials hold the real power and elected members are consulted, is a democratic anomaly that we have tolerated for far too long. Limerick voted for a directly elected mayor in 2019. That vote must be honoured, and the enabling legislation has been promised session after session. Where is it? When will it be published, and when will the people of Limerick actually get to elect their mayor? Beyond Limerick, the Government committed to considering plebiscites for Dublin and other cities. Dublin is one of very few capital cities in Europe without a directly accountable executive head. The consequences are visible: fragmented governance across four local authorities, no single figure accountable for the housing emergency or for transport, and decisions made by agencies that answer to nobody the public can name. I am not asking the Taoiseach for a philosophical reflection; I am asking for dates. When will the Limerick legislation be enacted? When will the plebiscites for the other cities be held? And will the offices created carry genuine powers over housing, transport and planning, with the funding to match? If devolution means anything, it means trusting citizens with these decisions, and I ask the Taoiseach to give the House a clear and specific answer today.

the collapse of the Soviet Union the greatest geopolitical catastrophe of the twentieth century. These are not the idle musings of a historian; they are the stated worldview of a man with a million men under arms and a demonstrated willingness to use them. When somebody tells us repeatedly who they are and what they intend, we should believe them. The pattern is consistent: Georgia in 2008, Crimea and the Donbas in 2014, the poisonings on our own soil, the cyber-attacks, the interference in democratic elections across the West. At each stage, the response of the democracies was strong words followed by weak actions, and at each stage the lesson drawn in Moscow was that aggression pays. Sanctions were imposed and then quietly eroded. Dependence on Russian gas deepened rather than diminished. London's markets and, I am sorry to say, London's lawyers and estate agents continued to welcome money whose provenance nobody cared to examine too closely. We in this House cannot condemn Putin's regime on Mondays and service its wealth on Tuesdays. That is why I support the measures before us, but I urge the Government to go further and faster on three fronts. First, the economic crime legislation this House has been promised for years must be brought forward without further delay, with a properly resourced register of overseas entities so that we know who owns what in this country. Second, we must accelerate the reduction of European dependence on Russian hydrocarbons, which funds the very war machine we deplore. Third, we must sustain our support - military, economic and humanitarian - for the sovereign right of Russia's neighbours to choose their own path. Deterrence is cheaper than war, but deterrence must be credible, and credibility is built from actions accumulated over years. We have years of accumulated inaction to make up for, and I fear we do not have years in which to do it.

self-employment. Bogus self-employment is not a technical quirk of the labour market; it is a deliberate business model that transfers risk from the employer to the worker and cost from the employer to the taxpayer. The worker loses sick pay, holiday pay, pension contributions and protection from unfair dismissal. The Exchequer loses national insurance revenue running into billions. And the honest employer, who engages staff properly and pays their dues, is undercut by the competitor who does not. The Taylor review reported in 2017. The Government accepted the diagnosis, promised an employment Bill, and have delivered precisely nothing. Queen's Speech after Queen's Speech, the employment Bill has been promised and postponed, while the case law has grown ever more tangled. We have had the Uber judgment from the Supreme Court, which confirmed what drivers had said all along - that they are workers, entitled to the minimum wage and holiday pay - but each such victory takes years of litigation that individual workers cannot afford, funded in that case by trade unions and fought against by companies with limitless legal budgets. Rights that must be litigated into existence one employer at a time are not rights at all in any practical sense. That is why statutory clarity matters. A single, clear definition of worker status, enforced proactively by a properly resourced state enforcement body rather than left to the bravery of individuals, would transform the position at a stroke. It would also, incidentally, be good for business: the good employer has nothing to fear from a level playing field, and everything to fear from a race to the bottom. So my question to the Minister is simple. The review is five years old. The promises are gathering dust. Where is the employment Bill, when will worker status be put on a statutory footing, and how many more years must people in insecure work wait for protections this House knows they need?

Let us go through some of the specifics, because the member's speech was long on grievance and remarkably short on numbers. The Canada summer jobs program is funding over 100,000 job placements this year, in every single riding represented in this House, including the member's own. I would wager he has attended announcements for those placements and been photographed doing so. We doubled the Canada student grant during the pandemic and have extended enhanced supports since, and we eliminated interest on federal student loans - a measure that saves the average borrower hundreds of dollars a year and that the member's party voted against. On housing, which I agree is the defining pressure on young Canadians, we have brought in the tax-free first home savings account, which hundreds of thousands of young people have already opened, and we are building more homes through agreements with municipalities that his party's leader has dismissed and voted against. On mental health, we have made the largest investments in youth mental health in federal history, working with provinces to reduce wait times. Now, I will grant the member this: the anxieties of young Canadians are real. The generation entering the workforce today faces a housing market and a cost of living their parents did not. But the answer to those anxieties is not slogans; it is sustained investment, and on every occasion this House has voted on such investment, the member and his colleagues have voted no. Young Canadians can judge for themselves the sincerity of a party that films videos about their struggles and then votes against every measure designed to address them. On this side of the House, we will keep delivering, and we welcome the comparison of records any day of the week.

Under the relevant legislation, where a property owned by an education and training board is no longer required for its original educational purpose, there is a defined process for determining its future use. The first consideration is whether there is an ongoing or emerging educational need in the area that the property could serve - for example, further education and training provision, a Youthreach centre, or accommodation for a school awaiting its permanent building. If no such need is identified, wider public uses can then be considered in consultation with other Departments and with the local authority. In the case of this property, that assessment is under way. I am aware of the strong local interest in the site, given its central location and the pressure on community facilities in a town that has grown as rapidly as Maynooth has. The Deputy will appreciate that Maynooth is one of the fastest-growing towns in the country, and the demand for school places, further education provision and community space has grown accordingly. I would caution against any assumption that the property will simply be disposed of on the open market; that is not the default outcome, and my strong preference, which I have communicated to the ETB, is that a property acquired and developed with public funds should continue to serve a public purpose. I expect the assessment to conclude in the coming months, and I have asked my officials to keep the Oireachtas members for the constituency informed. I would also encourage the local community groups that have expressed interest to make their proposals known formally to the ETB, so that the full range of options is on the table when the decision falls to be made.

The targets in Housing for All are floors, not ceilings, and the reality is that even if every target were met on schedule, we would still be playing catch-up on a decade of undersupply. The Central Bank, the ESRI and the Housing Commission have all indicated that real annual need is well above the published targets when pent-up demand, obsolescence and population growth are counted honestly. So delivery is the test, and delivery requires us to confront the bottlenecks frankly. The planning system remains too slow and too uncertain; a system in which strategic housing developments can sit in judicial review for years serves neither communities nor housebuilders. The capacity of the construction sector is constrained by labour shortages that will not resolve themselves; we need the apprenticeship pipeline expanded and we need targeted work permits, because we cannot build 40,000 homes a year with the workforce that struggled to build 20,000. The utilities - water and electricity connections - are now a genuine brake on delivery in parts of the country, and Uisce Éireann and the ESB must be funded and held to account accordingly. constituents in rural areas face round trips of several hours to attend hearings that may last twenty minutes, following the closure of their local courts - closures that were justified, at the time, on the promise that technology would fill the gap. The technology has arrived late and unevenly, and the buildings that were sold cannot be bought back. So while I welcome innovation in online procedures, I make this plea to the Minister: let online justice be an addition to access, not a substitute for presence. There are hearings for which video is perfectly adequate - case management, straightforward directions, matters between represented parties. But there are also hearings where physical presence matters profoundly: where a litigant is unrepresented and bewildered, where credibility is in issue, where a defendant needs to understand the gravity of the proceedings, or where a victim needs to see justice done in the flesh. The research from the early adoption of remote hearings should give us all pause - participants who did not understand what had happened to them, technical failures that fell hardest on the poorest, lawyers unable to take confidential instructions from their clients mid-hearing. Justice is not merely a transaction to be processed at the lowest unit cost; it is a public ritual through which the state demonstrates fairness, and rituals lose their force when reduced to a grid of faces on a screen. I therefore ask the Minister for three commitments: first, that the choice of a physical hearing remains a right, not a concession, wherever a party's effective participation requires it; second, that the court estate be protected from further closures until the online systems have been evaluated independently and in public; and third, that data on outcomes - not merely throughput - be collected and published, so that this House can judge whether online justice is delivering justice, and not merely delivering disposals.

The Good Friday Agreement's genius was to make the border irrelevant, allowing people to be British, Irish or both, and to live accordingly. Anything that rebuilds the border's salience unpicks that settlement thread by thread. So the Government must hold firm, and this House should be united in supporting that position - not out of any hostility to Britain, our nearest neighbour and closest friend, but out of fidelity to an agreement that ended a conflict which cost more than 3,000 lives. Let me walk through how the provisions interact, because it is important that the record is clear. Section 38 establishes the substantive protection: it sets out the circumstances in which a notice of termination is invalid and extends the notice periods according to the duration of the tenancy. Canadians are entitled to draw the obvious inference, and no amount of talking points about cabinet-making prerogatives will erase it. The rule of law in this country depends on a simple principle: prosecutorial decisions are made on the evidence and the law, not on the political interests of the government of the day, and the attorney general stands as the guardian of that boundary. When the guardian is punished for guarding, every future attorney general receives the message, and the boundary moves. That is why this matters far beyond the fate of any one company or any one minister. So the questions we are asking are simple ones. Who initiated the meetings? What was said? Why did the Prime Minister's most senior adviser and officials in his office consider it appropriate to raise, again and again, considerations that the law expressly excludes? Let the Prime Minister waive privilege fully - not partially, not selectively - and let every participant testify under oath before committee. If the government's conduct was as innocent as it claims, it has nothing to fear from sunlight. Its resistance to that sunlight is, at this point, the most eloquent testimony we have.

But I will not stand here and pretend the position is acceptable, because for the young people affected it is not. A driving licence is not a luxury; in large parts of the country it is the precondition of employment. The apprentice who cannot get to the site for a 7 am start, the care worker whose rounds cannot be done by bus, the young person in a rural area for whom every job advertisement says "must drive" - for them, every month of delay is a month of opportunity deferred. I have asked the agency to look specifically at that issue and at the practice of test slots being harvested by booking intermediaries and resold at a premium, which is profiteering from a public service backlog and which we are acting to curtail. My hon. This Bill is modest in its mechanics but significant in its meaning: it asks that Ireland, in its public procurement and trade, cease to treat goods produced in illegally occupied territories as though the occupation did not exist. The principle at stake could not be simpler. This State does not recognise the legality of settlements in occupied territories - that is the position of the Government, of the European Union and of international law as expressed by the International Court of Justice. Yet while we declare the settlements illegal, we permit trade in the goods they produce, and that contradiction hollows out our position. If it is wrong to build on confiscated land, it cannot be right to profit from what is grown and manufactured there. I have listened carefully to the objections. It is said the Bill conflicts with European Union competence on trade, and that Ireland cannot act alone. But the Attorney General's advice has never been published in full, and respected legal scholars have argued the contrary - that a narrowly drawn measure grounded in public policy exceptions is defensible. If the Government believes the legal position is truly prohibitive, let it publish the advice and let the Oireachtas judge. It is also said that the Bill would damage relations with allies. I would answer that Ireland's standing in the world - the moral capital we draw on when we speak on human rights at the United Nations, capital built by our peacekeepers and missionaries and aid workers over generations - depends precisely on our willingness to match words with actions when it costs us something. Small states do not shape the world through carrier groups; we shape it through consistency. I will support this Bill through the House, and I urge the Government, even now, to stop resisting it and start helping to perfect it.

A planning system that takes years to determine a major application serves no one - not the applicant, not the objector, not the environment and not the exchequer - but the cure for slow decisions is not fewer rights of participation; it is more planners. An Bord Pleanála has been operating far below its required complement of inspectors for years, and local authority planning departments have been hollowed out since the crash and never rebuilt. We can pass all the reforming legislation we like; if the desks are empty, the files will still sit in queues. Public participation is not the enemy of good development; it is one of its preconditions. The projects that get bogged down worst are very often those where consultation was treated as a formality - where communities learned the real details from the newspaper and turned to the courts because no one would engage with them earlier. Compare that with the projects, and there are good examples around the country, where developers engaged early and honestly, adjusted their proposals, and proceeded with community support and without a single judicial review. Genuine consultation is not a delay; it is insurance against delay. On judicial review itself, I accept there is an issue to be addressed, but the answer is to fix the underlying decision-making so that decisions are legally robust in the first place. Most successful challenges succeed because the decision was defective - because reports were inadequate or statutory requirements were skipped. Cure the defects and the challenges fail. Restrict access to the courts instead, and we will simply be building bad projects with less scrutiny, and storing up European law problems that will cost us far more time in the end. So the answer is capacity, quality and early engagement - not shortcuts. Shortcuts in planning have given this country flooded estates, pyrite and mica. We should have learned that lesson at sufficient cost by now.

No other country in Europe asked Ukrainians for visas. The European Union, not famed for the speed of its decision-making, activated the temporary protection directive within days, giving millions the immediate right to live, work and access services across twenty-six countries. We, by contrast, asked mothers with children who had slept in metro stations to fill in online forms, upload utility bills, and travel to visa application centres - and when the centre in Kyiv closed, we directed them to Warsaw and to Rzeszow, where the queues stretched into days. Members on all sides took calls from constituents trying to extract relatives through this labyrinth, and we all heard the same disbelief: this is Britain, they said; why is Britain doing this? When public pressure finally forced the schemes into being - the family scheme, then Homes for Ukraine - the generosity of the British people vastly outran the administration of the British state. Tens of thousands of families offered their spare rooms within days; the matching, the checks and the paperwork then took weeks while offers of sanctuary sat unused and the people they were meant for waited in borderland hostels. I recognise that the schemes have since scaled and that many have now arrived, and I welcome every single one. But the lesson must be learned and stated plainly: in an emergency of this kind, protection first and process second. That is what the temporary protection model does, and the Government should legislate now for an equivalent standing mechanism, so that the next crisis - and there will be a next crisis - is met with a system, not a scramble. Compassion delayed, for a refugee, is compassion denied, and my hon. Friend is right that we should ask ourselves hard questions about why the delay seemed tolerable this time.

The national children's hospital has become a byword for cost overrun - hundreds of millions beyond every estimate given to this House, with no one held accountable. The national broadband plan was signed at a multiple of the original costing against official advice. Money is always found for these things. Yet when the nurses sought pay restoration after years of emergency cuts, they were told about wage discipline. When carers - who save this State billions annually by looking after loved ones at home - sought a modest increase, they were told about fiscal space. When young teachers and gardaí on lower pay scales for the same work sought equality, they were told to wait for the next agreement, and then the one after that. That is the double standard at the heart of this Government's rhetoric on fiscal stability, and workers can see it plainly. Stability is not built by suppressing wages while the cost of housing devours whatever gains workers make. A worker's problem today is not their pay increase; it is that their rent absorbs it twice over. The State's failure on housing has become a machine for transferring workers' wages to landlords and funds, and then Ministers express surprise that pay demands persist. If the Government wants moderation from workers, it must deliver moderation in the cost of living - housing above all - and it must apply to its own capital projects the discipline it preaches to everyone else. Until then, lectures on fiscal stability from empty Government benches will convince nobody, and the absence of the Ministers today tells its own story about how seriously they take it.

The Bill before us matters to my constituents for a simple reason: connectivity is the difference between a community that keeps its young people and one that waves them off. I represent towns that were promised much when the railways were reorganised, promised more when the franchises changed hands, and promised again at each new investment announcement - and which still wait on platforms for trains that are late, short-formed or cancelled. The economic literature on this is not contested: transport investment concentrates where activity already concentrates, and activity concentrates where transport is invested. Left to the market's own logic, that circle never breaks. It takes deliberate public choice to break it, and that is what I am asking for. The measures in this Bill on accountability are welcome so far as they go. Passengers need a single body that answers when things go wrong, rather than the current carousel in which the operator blames the infrastructure, the infrastructure blames the funding settlement, and the Minister blames the operator with a straight face. But accountability without investment is a complaints procedure, not a railway. So I want to press the Minister on three specifics: the timetable for the upgrades promised to my region, in months and years rather than in adjectives; a fares structure that does not punish the flexible worker, because the season ticket assumptions of 1995 do not describe the labour market of today; and accessibility, because a station without step-free access is, for many of my constituents, not a station at all. The hon. Severe mental illness - schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, severe depression with psychosis - affects a minority, but for that minority and their families it is utterly life-altering, and the gap between what we promise and what we provide is nowhere wider. People with severe mental illness die, on average, fifteen to twenty years earlier than the general population, overwhelmingly from treatable physical conditions - a mortality gap that has barely narrowed in a generation. If any other patient group faced that statistic, it would headline every news bulletin. The wider conversation about mental wellbeing over the past decade has done real good: stigma has genuinely receded, and people speak of anxiety and depression in ways unthinkable when I entered this House. But my hon. Friend is right that there is a risk in that success - the risk that resources and attention flow toward the accessible end of the spectrum, the apps and awareness campaigns, while the acutely unwell wait days in accident and emergency departments for a psychiatric bed, or are sent hundreds of miles from home because no local bed exists. Out-of-area placements were supposed to be eliminated; they persist. The early intervention in psychosis standards are met in some areas and missed in others, a postcode lottery in the one intervention with the strongest evidence of changing life trajectories. Community mental health teams carry caseloads that make continuity of care - the single thing patients and families most value - impossible. So while I welcome the funding commitments and the reforms to the Mental Health Act, which are overdue and humane, the test I will apply is concrete: fewer out-of-area placements, shorter waits for a bed, physical health checks actually delivered for people on severe mental illness registers, and support for the families - the carers - who hold this system together at enormous personal cost and are consulted by it almost never. That is the unfinished business, and I am grateful to my hon. Friend for keeping the House's attention upon it.

We have a teacher supply crisis in particular subjects and particular areas - that is not disputed by anybody who looks at the vacancy lists - and at the same time we have qualified teachers, trained in other jurisdictions, living in Ireland and unable to stand in front of a class because their paperwork is moving through a process that can take many months. That is a failure of administration, not a protection of standards. Nobody in this House is suggesting that we compromise on the quality of the profession; Irish education ranks where it does precisely because entry to teaching is demanding, and that must remain so. But there is a world of difference between maintaining standards and maintaining queues. The Teaching Council's registration process for teachers qualified abroad involves assessments of qualifications, vetting, and in some cases requirements for additional modules or Irish-language conditions for particular settings. Each element is defensible; their cumulative duration is not. A teacher from Canada or New Zealand - jurisdictions whose education systems are hardly suspect - can wait the better part of a year while principals in Dublin and in rural areas alike are cancelling classes or collapsing them together for want of a body in front of the room. And each of those teachers has a choice of countries competing for them; every month of delay is a month in which England or Australia makes them a faster offer. So the specific proposals I have put to the Minister are these: a fast-track registration channel for teachers from jurisdictions whose qualifications frameworks we already recognise; provisional registration allowing supervised classroom work while final requirements are completed; and published service standards for the Teaching Council with quarterly reporting on processing times. None of this requires legislation; it requires direction and resources. The children in classrooms without a permanent teacher this term cannot wait for a perfect system, and I would ask the Minister to treat this with the urgency the vacancy figures demand.

we have heard repeatedly in this debate, the current arrangement is itself the greater incentive to enter the informal economy, which is precisely where exploitation flourishes. Consider the actual position of a person in the asylum system today. They wait many months - very often more than a year - for an initial decision. During that time they are prohibited from working, sustained on an allowance of a few pounds a day, housed where they are told, and forbidden from contributing the skills that many of them - doctors, engineers, care workers - arrived with. We then express surprise when some drift into illegal work, where there is no minimum wage, no safety inspection and no recourse against abuse. The policy manufactures the very shadow economy it claims to deter. The evidence from comparable countries is instructive: most of our European neighbours grant the right to work after six months or sooner, and there is no serious evidence that it acts as a magnet - study after study finds that asylum seekers' choice of destination is driven by language, family ties and perceived safety, not by fine distinctions in labour market rules that most could not recite. What the right to work demonstrably does is reduce the welfare bill, increase tax revenue, preserve skills and mental health, and improve integration outcomes for those ultimately granted protection - which, we should remember, is the majority of applicants under the current grant rates. The Lords amendment is modest: the right to work only after six months of Home Office delay, in other words only where the state itself has failed to decide in time. If the Government dislike the amendment, there is a remedy entirely within their control: decide cases within six months, and the right never crystallises. I gently say to my hon. Friend the Minister that a policy defensible only if we never fix the backlog is not a policy; it is an alibi, and I shall support the Lords amendment tonight.

The system we have is, in essence, one of self-certification by parties engaged and paid by the developer. The assigned certifier is appointed by the builder or developer, the inspections are arranged within that commercial relationship, and the State's role - through the local building control authorities - amounts to a very limited level of inspection coverage. Local authority building control functions were decimated during the austerity years and have never been restored to anything approaching adequacy: the number of qualified building control officers across the State would fit comfortably into this committee room. We inspect a small percentage of construction activity and rely on statutory declarations for the rest. The consequences of that architecture are written across the country: Priory Hall, Longboat Quay, the pyrite estates, the mica homes, the apartment blocks whose owners are now levied tens of thousands of euro each for fire safety defects that certified compliance concealed. In every case there were certificates; in every case the certificates were worth less than the paper. Homeowners did everything right - they bought completed, certified properties - and they have carried the cost while those who signed the certificates have, in the main, faced no consequence, their companies dissolved and their insurance disclaiming liability. That is why I have consistently argued for an independent building control inspectorate - inspectors employed by the State or by local authorities, funded by a levy on construction, inspecting at defined stages with the power to halt works - as exists in other jurisdictions. It is also why the defective blocks and apartment remediation schemes, necessary as they are, must be accompanied by a latent defects insurance requirement and a register of certifiers with real disciplinary teeth. The taxpayer keeps paying to remediate what proper inspection would have prevented. Reform costs a fraction of remediation, and I would ask the Minister to bring forward the heads of a Bill this year.

Let us be honest about what the childcare sector actually is. It is the infrastructure on which the entire working economy stands - no childcare, no workforce - and it is staffed overwhelmingly by qualified, dedicated women who are paid barely above the minimum wage despite holding degrees and diplomas in early years education. The average wage in the sector is a scandal. Staff love the work and love the children, but love does not pay rent, and so they leave - for the schools as SNAs, for retail, for anywhere that pays better - and every departure means a room closed, a waiting list lengthened, a parent unable to take up work. Providers, meanwhile, are caught in an impossible vice: parents are already paying fees that rival a mortgage, so fees cannot rise, while costs - insurance, heating, food, rent - climb relentlessly. In rural areas like Kerry the position is more precarious again, because smaller services lack the scale to absorb shocks, and when the only service in a village closes, there is no alternative down the road; there is simply no childcare, and usually it is the mother who gives up work. The core funding model was meant to address this, and it has helped, but the numbers before the House show services still closing and staff still leaving. So this motion's demands are ones I fully support: a workforce pay deal that reflects qualifications, a capital programme for rural provision, and a continued path towards a genuinely public model in which childcare is treated like education - a public good, publicly guaranteed. The providers in Kilgarvan and across Kerry are doing their part. It is time this House did its part by them.

Let us recall what we were told: that testing and tracing would be the bedrock of the reopening, that we would have capacity of a hundred thousand tests a week, that turnaround times would be measured in hours, not days. Now examine the reality: people waiting the better part of a week from referral to test, and days more for a result, while continuing - in some cases - to go about their business because the message on self-isolation has been muddled from the start. A test result delivered ten days after symptoms is not disease surveillance; it is history. Contact tracing conducted at that remove chases a virus that has already moved on twice. Every phase of the roadmap depends on this system functioning, because reopening without functioning surveillance is not a plan; it is a hope. The countries that have reopened successfully - and we should learn without embarrassment from South Korea and others - did so on the back of testing and tracing that operates in real time, and they built that capacity in weeks, not months. We have the laboratories, we have the scientists - the universities offered their capacity early on and were left waiting for calls back - and we have, in the contact tracing centres, willing staff who report being underused and stood down while the backlog persisted elsewhere in the chain. The failure is one of organisation and accountability: too many bodies, no single named person responsible for the end-to-end turnaround time. So I ask the Minister today for three commitments: a published end-to-end turnaround target of 24 hours from referral to result communicated; weekly publication of performance against that target, region by region; and a single accountable lead for the entire testing and tracing system. Without that, the roadmap is a calendar, not a plan.

Mr. Speaker, the reason this motion matters is written in the pay stubs of tens of thousands of public servants who, years after the Phoenix system was launched, are still being paid incorrectly - overpaid, underpaid or not paid at all. Let us remember how we got here. A pay system was procured with the promise of savings, launched against the advice of officials who warned it was not ready, and the people who processed pay under the old system were let go before the new one was proven. The result has been one of the most expensive administrative failures in the history of the federal government: billions of dollars spent stabilizing a system that was supposed to save hundreds of millions, a queue of pay issues that at its peak counted in the hundreds of thousands, and human costs that no ledger captures - families denied mortgages because income could not be verified, new parents with benefits miscalculated, employees driven to hardship funds because their own employer could not pay them for work performed. The Auditor General has reported on this repeatedly, and the public accounts committee has heard testimony that would be comical if it were not so costly. The lesson of Phoenix is that governance failures, not technical failures, sit at the root: unclear accountability, optimism presented as planning, and warnings filtered out before they reached decision-makers. That is why this motion insists on governance mechanisms engaging senior representatives of every concerned department - not working groups reporting to working groups, but named senior officials who own the outcome. The next-generation system will serve hundreds of thousands of employees. If we replicate the governance of Phoenix, we will replicate the results of Phoenix, and no member of this House, of any party, could look a public servant in the eye having allowed that. I urge the House to adopt the motion.

The principle is one I believe every Member of this House can stand over: those who serve the public - paramedics, nurses, gardaí, firefighters, prison officers and retail workers who enforced public health rules through the pandemic - are entitled to the strongest protection the law can give them, because an attack on them is an attack on the service they provide to all of us. The figures should stop us in our tracks. Assaults on emergency workers have risen year on year. Ambulance crews describe being called to scenes and pelted with missiles; emergency department nurses describe violence as a normal feature of a Saturday shift; and gardaí, whose assault numbers are published annually, face spitting, biting and worse as a matter of routine. Behind each statistic is a person who went to work to help people and came home injured, or did not come home at all, and behind them is a family that carries the fear on every subsequent shift. Increased penalties send an important signal of societal condemnation, and I support them without reservation. But I want to be honest with the House: sentencing alone will not solve this. Certainty of prosecution matters more than severity of sentence, and too many of these assaults never result in charges because the worker is discouraged from pursuing a complaint, or the case is dealt with as a minor public order matter. So alongside this Bill, we need a policy of presumptive prosecution for assaults on front-line workers, proper aftercare and compensation for those injured, and data published by each service so we can see whether we are succeeding. I also ask the Minister to examine the position of retail and transport workers, who face similar violence with fewer protections. I commend my colleagues in the Regional Group for the Bill, and I urge the Government to give it a speedy passage.

One in eight Christians worldwide now lives in a country where they may face persecution for their faith - discrimination in education and employment at the milder end, and at the harsher end, imprisonment, forced conversion, the burning of churches and murder. And, of course, Christians are not alone: the Uyghur Muslims in Xinjiang, the Rohingya, the Yazidis, the Baha'i in Iran and humanists and atheists in many states face the same machinery of persecution, and freedom of religion or belief - including the freedom to have no belief - is indivisible. If we defend it only for those who share our own traditions, we do not really believe in it at all. The Bishop of Truro's review, which the Government commissioned and accepted in full, set out a serious programme: naming freedom of religion or belief as a foreign policy priority, imposing sanctions on the worst persecutors, and ensuring that our aid programmes do not inadvertently discriminate against persecuted minorities in the distribution of relief - a real and documented problem, since aid delivered through local structures can replicate local exclusions. My questions to the Minister are therefore specific. How many of the Truro recommendations have been implemented in full - not "in progress", but done? On how many occasions have Magnitsky-style sanctions been applied specifically for religious persecution? What assessment has been made of aid distribution in countries where persecuted minorities report exclusion from relief? And will the Government commit to maintaining the special envoy role with proper resourcing and direct access to the Foreign Secretary? Open Doors and organisations like it do the painstaking work of documentation at real risk to their local partners. The least we owe them is that their evidence changes our policy, rather than merely adorning our debates. Persecution flourishes where the world looks away, and this House, at least, must keep looking.

That is a shameful inversion of the truth, and it matters that we say so plainly, because this narrative - seeded by the Kremlin and repeated by useful voices across the political spectrum, from certain corners of the left to certain corners of the right - is doing real work in corroding Western support for Ukraine. Let us state the facts. Ukraine is a sovereign nation. Its people have voted, repeatedly and in ever greater numbers, for a European future. The EU did not march anyone anywhere: association agreements are negotiated, signed and ratified by elected governments, and the crime for which Ukraine is being punished is precisely that choice. To suggest that Brussels provoked the invasion by offering Ukrainians trade and visa-free travel is to say that Ukraine's neighbours are entitled to a veto over its democracy - a doctrine of spheres of influence that Europe buried, or should have buried, in the twentieth century. And it insults the dead. The people murdered in Bucha were not killed by EU enlargement. The children abducted to Russia - in their thousands, a documented war crime - were not abducted because of a trade agreement. The apartment blocks in Mariupol were not flattened by NATO expansion. They were destroyed by an imperial project, explicitly articulated by Putin himself in his essays and speeches, which denies that Ukraine is a nation at all. Those on the left who repeat the provocation narrative should ask themselves what exactly is left-wing about excusing an imperialist war of conquest against a smaller neighbour, waged by a regime that murders trade unionists and journalists. Solidarity - the oldest value of the labour movement - lies with the Ukrainian people, their trade unions, their railway workers who evacuated millions under fire. Ireland, as a militarily neutral country, is not politically neutral between the aggressor and the victim, and neither should any democrat be.

have been telling us that the Canada Revenue Agency is failing at the most basic elements of its job. Call centre wait times stretch for hours, and when Canadians finally get through, the agency's own internal audits have found that a troubling share of the answers given are simply wrong. Think about that: a taxpayer does their duty, calls the government for guidance, waits half a day on hold, receives incorrect information, files accordingly - and is then penalized for the error. The agency makes the mistake; the Canadian pays the price. Small business owners tell me they must hire accountants not because their affairs are complicated but because dealing with the CRA has become a specialized skill. Seniors tell me about benefits clawed back without clear explanation and about letters so incomprehensible that they arrive at my constituency office in tears, afraid they have done something wrong when in fact they have done everything right. Meanwhile, the same agency that cannot answer a phone call from a waitress about her T4 has shown remarkable energy pursuing ordinary Canadians for modest sums, while - as the public accounts and the Auditor General have shown - large-scale offshore avoidance identified in successive leaks has produced strikingly few convictions. The double standard is glaring: relentless efficiency toward the small and the compliant, endless patience toward the large and the lawyered. This is a solvable problem. Fix the phone lines with published service standards and real accountability when they are missed. Write correspondence in plain language - other tax authorities have done it. Give the taxpayers' ombudsperson real teeth. Institute a simple rule of fairness: where a taxpayer relies in good faith on written or recorded CRA guidance, the penalty is waived. And redirect enforcement resources up the income scale to where the actual money is. Canadians are honest; they will do their part. It is time the agency did its part, and I hope members opposite will support the motion before the House today.

Trump has described journalists as the enemy of the people, has revoked credentials from outlets whose questions he dislikes, and has worked systematically to delegitimise every institution capable of holding him to account. When the Taoiseach of Ireland, in New York of all places, offers even a wry note of sympathy with that worldview - musing about unfair coverage and journalists with agendas - it travels. It is heard by every government on earth looking for respectable cover for muzzling its press, and it is heard at home by a media sector already under severe strain. Let us speak about that strain, because it is the real issue beneath this exchange. Media plurality in Ireland is in a precarious state: local newspapers are closing or hollowed out, ownership is concentrated to a degree that previous Oireachtas reports have flagged as a democratic concern, RTÉ lurches from funding crisis to funding crisis without a decision from Government on the licence fee, and the advertising revenue that once sustained journalism has migrated to two or three platforms that bear none of journalism's costs and few of its responsibilities. The Future of Media Commission was established, it reported, and its central recommendations have sat unimplemented while the Government cherry-picks around the edges. A functioning democracy requires journalists who can afford to spend months on a story, court reporters in every circuit, local papers at every council meeting - the daily, unglamorous scrutiny that keeps power honest. That infrastructure is collapsing quietly while we debate the Taoiseach's remarks. So I ask him to do two things. First, state without qualification, here in this House, that a free and often infuriating press is a cornerstone of Irish democracy and that he rejects the characterisation of the media as an enemy. Second, bring forward the funding decisions - on the licence fee, on the media fund, on local journalism schemes - that his own commission recommended. Warm words about press freedom, from a Government starving the press of the means to be free, will convince no one.

That asymmetry is the heart of the issue I am raising, because it means the national fleet, which is meant to serve the whole country, is being drawn systematically into covering capacity gaps in the capital, and the areas that pay the price are the very counties with the longest baseline response times already. The capacity review told us plainly that the NAS requires a substantial increase in staffing and vehicles to meet demand safely, so my questions to the Minister are these. This is the absurdity at the heart of the matter: the State has invested hundreds of millions of euro in flood defences, the defences demonstrably work, and the insurance industry continues to rate the protected areas as though the walls and embankments did not exist. The memorandum of understanding between Insurance Ireland and the OPW was supposed to resolve exactly this - the OPW provides the industry with detailed data on completed schemes and the standard of protection they provide, and insurers in return are supposed to reflect that protection in underwriting. The industry's own figures claim high levels of cover in areas protected by fixed defences, but those claims dissolve on contact with reality: they conflate any cover with flood cover, they count policies with flood risk excluded, and where demountable defences are involved - as in several towns in my constituency - many insurers simply refuse cover outright, despite those defences having performed flawlessly in every deployment. The consequence for my constituents is severe and compounding: homes that cannot be insured cannot be mortgaged, homes that cannot be mortgaged cannot be sold, and a family's principal asset is quietly stranded through no fault of their own, after the State has already spent the money that should have solved the problem. So I am asking the Minister of State for three things: publication, scheme by scheme, of insurance uptake data in protected areas, independently verified rather than industry self-reported; a review of the memorandum with real consequences for non-compliance, because a voluntary arrangement that is ignored is not an arrangement at all; and, if the industry will not move, examination of the models used elsewhere - Flood Re in Britain being the obvious example - so that people living behind proven defences can insure their homes like anyone else.

debate a new framework for British agriculture in peacetime. Whatever our divisions over how we arrived at this moment, the opportunity itself should not be squandered, and it is in that spirit that I approach the Bill. The 1947 Act was designed for a country that had known rationing - its purpose was production above all, and it succeeded so well that within a generation we were grappling with surpluses. The common agricultural policy that followed paid farmers substantially for the acreage they held, a system whose defects were rehearsed for decades: the greatest subsidies flowing to the largest landowners, tenant farmers and smallholders scraping by, and environmental harm subsidised at public expense. The principle at the heart of this Bill - public money for public goods - is therefore right, and I support it. Paying farmers for what markets cannot pay them for - soil health, flood management, biodiversity, access to the countryside - is a sound foundation. But a sound principle can be wrecked by careless transition, and my concerns are practical. First, the seven-year transition assumes the new environmental schemes will be ready, comprehensible and adequately funded as the old payments taper; the pilots to date do not yet justify that confidence, and a farmer cannot run a business on a scheme that exists mainly in consultation documents. Second, food security has slipped too far down the order of priorities; public goods must include the strategic capacity to feed ourselves, a lesson the pandemic has just retaught us. Third, standards: it would be an act of self-harm to demand higher environmental and welfare standards of our own farmers while signing trade agreements that admit food produced to standards that would be illegal here. That undercuts the very farmers this Bill asks to do more. I shall table amendments on those points, but I welcome the chance - denied to every Member under 93, as I say - to shape what farming in this country is for.

Home ownership - and secure, affordable renting alongside it - is the foundation on which stable families, stable communities and, yes, stable democracies are built. A generation that can never own anything, that moves rental to rental at a landlord's notice, that postpones children because a two-bedroom flat consumes both salaries, is a generation with no stake in the system we ask them to defend. We should not be surprised when they conclude the system is not worth defending, and we should not lecture them about radicalism when it was our failure that radicalised them. The causes are not mysterious; they have been documented in report after report. We do not build enough homes, and we have not for forty years. The planning system rewards those who already own and organises itself against those who do not: every proposal is met by objectors whose houses are already built, and the political incentives at local level all point toward refusal. Infrastructure lags where housing is permitted; housing is refused where infrastructure exists. And the subsidies we do provide too often inflate demand against a fixed supply, enriching sellers in the name of helping buyers. The remedies flow from the diagnosis: build - publicly and privately - at a scale not seen since the postwar decades; reform planning so that the presumption favours homes, with communities given a genuine share of the gains rather than only the disruption; invest in the infrastructure first so that consent follows; and protect renters properly in the meantime, because the meantime is where millions of people live. Every part of that will offend somebody, which is precisely why it has not been done. But the alternative is a country that tells its young people it has no room for them, and no party - mine included - deserves to survive on that platform.

Now, I want to be careful and fair, because the picture is contested. Universities point out that the number of speaker events actually cancelled is small, and that is true as far as it goes. The university is the one institution in society whose entire purpose is the disciplined collision of ideas; if orthodoxy has a sanctuary anywhere, it must not be there. That is why I support the Bill's provisions strengthening the duty to secure free speech, including for visiting speakers, and placing that duty on students' unions as well. But a Gladue report is a dead letter where a mandatory minimum applies: the judge may read it, may be moved by it, and must then impose the same sentence regardless. We ask judges to weigh context and then we handcuff the scale. The government promised comprehensive reform. What it delivered repealed some minimums - and I supported that - but left many standing, including provisions under which the very women I am describing continue to be sentenced. Court after court has struck these provisions down as cruel and unusual, meaning we are maintaining, piecemeal, a sentencing regime the Constitution keeps rejecting, at enormous cost in litigation and in human lives. I want to make the substantive case as well as the procedural one: the clinical arguments for centralisation, valid as they may be for complex surgery, are routinely over-applied to services - step-down care, respite, rehabilitation, minor injuries - where distance itself is a clinical risk. An elderly patient recovering forty miles from their family recovers more slowly and is discharged into worse support. A carer who cannot reach the respite unit stops using respite, and then the caring arrangement collapses, and the State pays for a nursing home place that proper local provision would have made unnecessary. I do not take the setting aside of convention lightly. The conventions of this House are not decoration; they are the accumulated wisdom of centuries about how a legislature and an executive share power without paralysis, and I have defended them throughout my time here, sometimes against my own party's convenience. Those who warn that today's procedural innovation becomes tomorrow's precedent are right, and I will not pretend otherwise. But conventions exist to serve parliamentary government, not to disarm it, and when an executive uses the control of the Order Paper - itself a convention - to prevent the House from expressing its view on the gravest peacetime decision in generations, it is the Government, not this motion, that has broken the constitutional bargain. The House is not seeking to govern; it is seeking to decide, which is precisely what Members are sent here to do. My constituents did not elect me to be a spectator at their own future. The businesses in my constituency - I have sat with them, gone through their order books and their contingency plans - tell me in plain terms what an abrupt rupture would mean: contracts lost, lines stopped for want of components, produce rotting at ports. Those are not projections from think-tanks; they are the arithmetic of firms that employ my neighbours. Faced with that, and with the clock running down, the question before each of us is simple: does the House take responsibility, or does it avert its eyes and call the aversion principle? I say this to colleagues on my own Benches who share my unease about the method: the way to make today's procedure unnecessary is for the Government to give the House the votes it should have offered freely. Until it does, I will support motions like this one - with sadness, as I said, but without apology, because the deepest convention of all is that Parliament decides.
