Families report that in a matter of months they have lost the person twice - once to the isolation and once, when the doors finally open, to the stranger the isolation left behind. I do not stand here to attack care homes; managers are terrified of an outbreak and are following guidance that shifts beneath their feet, and their staff have been heroic. Nor do I dismiss the risk; my own constituency has buried too many. But a policy that treats every visit as an equal hazard, regardless of testing, PPE or the visitor's role in the resident's care, is not caution - it is a failure to weigh one harm against another. Other countries have designated essential family caregivers, tested and equipped like staff, with regular access. The technology exists, the protocols exist, and the pilot schemes here have shown it can be done safely. By the time the loaf of bread and the pound of butter reach the shelf, the taxes levied in the name of climate policy have been baked into the price several times over, and it is the pensioner and the family on a tight budget who pay the compound total. And for what? The farmer has no electric tractor to switch to; there is none on the market that can do the work. The haulier has no electric lorry that can do the Cork to Dublin run fully loaded. A tax that is meant to change behaviour, applied to people who have no alternative behaviour available, is not an environmental policy; it is simply revenue, collected disproportionately from rural Ireland. So I say to the Minister: suspend the carbon tax increases on agricultural diesel and marked fuel until genuine alternatives exist; apply the fuel excise reductions for as long as prices remain at crisis levels, not on a cliff-edge timetable; and examine the VAT-on-excise anomaly that every fuel retailer in the country can explain in thirty seconds. The Government cannot tell farmers to produce more food and simultaneously tax the very means of producing it beyond reach. That is not a climate strategy; it is a contradiction, and rural Ireland is being asked to pay for it.

I want to make three points in the time available. First, we should finally honour the commitment, made by successive Governments across five decades, to reach 0.7% of national income. We have crept upwards, and the increases in recent budgets are welcome, but at the current pace the target recedes as the economy grows. A country running budget surpluses, which lectures others on the rules-based order, should meet the oldest promise on its books; certainty of trajectory matters as much to programme planning as the destination itself. Second, we must protect the character of the programme as it grows. The pressure on every donor country is to bend aid towards migration management, trade promotion and strategic visibility. Irish Aid's authority rests precisely on its refusal to be bent; poverty reduction is the mandate, and this House should guard it jealously. Third, coherence: it makes little sense to build climate resilience in the Horn of Africa with one hand while our wider policies work against those same communities with the other, and the commitments on climate finance must be genuinely additional, not repackaged from the existing envelope. Development aid is not charity; it is the most concrete expression of the values this State claims for itself, and - as the Deputy said - it is one field where an honest observer can say the Government has largely got it right. That is the legacy I mean, and it does not happen by accident. It happens if, and only if, it is written into the procurement: apprenticeship requirements in every major contract, work packages sized so that small specialist firms can bid rather than being swallowed as sub-sub-contractors, training academies established in the regions where the fabrication will actually be done, and targets published and reported against annually to this House. The precedents are there - the Olympic park showed what deliberate skills procurement can achieve, and the cathedral workshops of this country and of Europe show how craft skills survive: through institutions that commit for decades, not through projects that commit for a contract cycle. So my questions to the Minister are these: will the delivery authority be given an explicit statutory or contractual mandate for skills and apprenticeships; will the regional distribution of work and training be reported publicly; and will the House be given, before the main works contracts are let, a skills legacy plan we can scrutinise? We are the temporary custodians of this building. The masons who built it trained the masons who maintained it; we owe the next century's craftsmen the same inheritance.
